lessons.title: From many-body energy levels to adding and removing spectra
lessons.summary: The energy difference between adjacent particle number sectors determines the peak position, and the electronic operator matrix element determines whether the peak is visible.

sections.title: Select one operator for one measurement
sections.text: The initial state is fixed N↑, N↓. Adding an up-spin electron takes the system into the (N↑+1,N↓) sector, removing it takes it into (N↑−1,N↓). Therefore, all energy levels in the same N sector cannot be directly regarded as photoelectron peaks; truly visible transitions require non-zero creation or annihilation operator matrix elements.

sections.title: Energy zero point and electron number are two settings
sections.text: The horizontal axis uses energy instead of angular frequency, in eV. μ is only subtracted from the positions of all single-particle peaks, without changing the fixed electron number or occupation of the initial state. Any μ does not guarantee that the added spectrum will be on the positive half-axis and the removed spectrum will be on the negative half-axis; the button to move μ cannot be interpreted as automatic doping.

sections.title: Local probe and Fourier probe see different weights
sections.text: The local probe of this site acts on one site; the Fourier probe is the normalized superposition of the amplitudes of all sites. For open dimers, the q=0 combination selects the bonding orbital, and the q a/π=1 combination selects the antibonding orbital. The q in the open chain represents the probe phase, which cannot be regarded as a strictly periodic crystal momentum quantum number.

sections.title: The same set of poles gives Green's function and spectral function
sections.text: Real and imaginary parts of the retarded Green function come from the same discrete transitions. η>0 imposes the correct retarded boundary condition and produces Lorentzian line shapes. Matrix elements determine peak areas, while peak heights also depend on η. This computes finite-cluster single-particle spectra without orbital dipole matrix elements or instrument geometry of actual photoemission experiments.

lessons.title: From equal-time correlations to dynamical spin and charge response
lessons.summary: The same Hamiltonian can be detected by different operators; compare the spin peak, charge peak and single particle peak of the number of adjacent particles.

sections.title: response maintains the total number of particles
sections.text: Density and longitudinal spin operators do not add or remove electrons, and the response final state of this module remains in the same (N↑,N↓) sector. Longitudinal spin adopts S_z=(n↑−n↓)/2 and ℏ=1. What is output here is the dynamic structure factor type spectrum S(q,E), which is not an unexplained complex magnetic susceptibility, nor is it automatically multiplied by 3 to become a complete vector spin spectrum.

sections.title: Subtract the mean before calculating a connected response
sections.text: Use δO=O−⟨O⟩I to remove the coherent average background. For fixed N, the total density connected spectrum of q=0 must disappear; for fixed N↑, N↓, the total S_z connected spectrum of q=0 also disappears. The program uses these two conservation limits as physical checks instead of artificially deleting peaks that it does not want to display.

sections.title: spin peak and charge peak answer different questions
sections.text: The q a/π=1 longitudinal-spin probe of a symmetric half-filled dimer connects its singlet ground state to the triplet; the charge probe connects to the odd-parity doubly occupied state. With D=√(U²+16t²), the peak energies are (D−U)/2 and (D+U)/2, respectively. Although both follow from the same Hamiltonian, they are not one universal gap.

sections.title: Integrating the dynamical spectrum recovers equal-time fluctuations
sections.text: Summing over a complete set of final states makes the total discrete transition weight equal to the connected equal-time correlation in the initial state. This links the Hubbard-correlation lesson to the dynamic spectrum. A degenerate ground space is treated with an equally weighted trace. Any fluctuations between zero-energy ground states also contribute to the sum rule; keeping only positive-energy peaks does not give the complete integral.

lessons.title: Test spectra using sum rules, degenerate averages and limits
lessons.summary: Distinguish discrete weights, line widths, sampling and physical conclusions, and observe the true zero-energy fluctuations of the degenerate initial state.

sections.title: The total weight of a normalized Fermi probe is 1
sections.text: Each calculation selects one spin and one normalized probe. Fermionic anticommutation gives removal weight n and addition weight 1−n, summing to 1. Do not add an unexplained spin factor or use identical normalization for a local spectrum and a density of states summed over all sites.

sections.title: The degenerate state requires tracing the subspace
sections.text: The initial state is equally weighted within the tolerance of the selected sector 10⁻⁹ eV, and the final state is summed according to the degenerate energy level group. This way the weights do not depend on the numerical diagonalization of an optional degenerate basis. After clicking on a spectrum peak, the final state density uses P_f Oρ₀O†P_f/w_f; it reflects the conditional final state actually reached by the probe and is not necessarily equal to the equal-weighted average of the entire final state energy level group.

sections.title: Strict atomic limits preserve zero energy fluctuations
sections.text: For a dimer with t=0, U>0 and (N↑,N↓)=(1,1), the two separated-occupancy configurations are degenerate. The q a/π=1 S_z probe takes opposite values in them, with mean zero but mean square 1/2. The connected spectrum therefore retains a zero-energy peak of weight 1/2: subtracting the mean does not remove every zero-energy response. This does not establish long-range magnetic order.

sections.title: Linewidth and plotting grids cannot create new physics
sections.text: η is the plotted Lorentzian half width at half maximum, not a physical lifetime calculated here. Discrete peak weights obey exact sum rules; a finite plot window omits Lorentzian tails, which are reported without renormalization. Energy spacing greater than η/3 triggers a peak-height undersampling warning. Finite spectra of two to four sites do not directly establish an infinite material’s phase diagram.

lessons.title: Let electrons and local oscillators enter the same quantum model
lessons.summary: Distinguish site-energy coupling, bond coupling and phonon energy. Establish a reference from the uncoupled limit.

sections.title: From two independent curves to a common state
sections.text: An electron hops between two local orbitals, with a quantum harmonic oscillator on each site. The complete basis labels the electron site and both phonon occupation numbers. One electron and its spin component are fixed; electron–electron repulsion is excluded.

sections.title: Holstein coupling changes site energies
sections.text: When an electron occupies a site, displacement of that site's oscillator changes its local electronic energy. The hopping t remains constant. The oscillator coordinate X is dimensionless; no conversion from mass and frequency to length has been specified, so numerical X values cannot simply be called Å.
sections.formula: H=−t(c_0†c_1+c_1†c_0)+Δ(n_0−n_1)/2+ℏω Σ_i b_i†b_i+g Σ_i n_i X_i；X_i=b_i+b_i†

sections.title: First check g=0
sections.text: Without coupling, the electronic two-level spectrum and the two oscillator spectra simply add. For Δ=0 and t>0, the ground state is the electronic bonding state times both oscillator vacua. The total  phonon  number is zero and the reduced electronic purity is 1; this does not mean that oscillator coordinates have no zero-point fluctuations.

sections.title: Connections to the existing SSH and phonon lessons
sections.text: A local Holstein displacement modulates the site energy, whereas an SSH-type bond displacement modulates hopping. Existing SSH bond parameters cannot be used directly as g here, and Phonopy frequencies do not automatically determine electron–phonon matrix elements. Compare the mechanisms while defining their parameters separately.

lessons.title: A uniform electron density can still hide a vibrational cloud
lessons.summary: From displaced oscillators in the atomic limit to electron–phonon correlations in a symmetric ground state.

sections.title: Complete the square directly in the atomic limit
sections.text: At t=0, first fix the site occupied by the electron. The occupied oscillator's potential-energy surface is displaced, lowering its ground-state energy by g²/(ℏω), with mean phonon number [g/(ℏω)]². Positive g gives negative X displacement. The total zero-point energy ℏω of the two oscillators has been omitted.

sections.title: An average distribution does not replace a correlation
sections.text: When Δ=0 and the ground state is nondegenerate, site-exchange symmetry requires both electronic occupations to equal 1/2. The electron and its accompanying vibrational cloud can delocalize together, so uniform density does not exclude electron– phonon  correlations. This two-site result cannot establish a self-trapping phase transition in an infinite crystal.
sections.formula: ⟨n_0⟩=⟨n_1⟩=1/2; in general, ⟨n_i X_j⟩ is not equal to ⟨n_i⟩⟨X_j⟩

sections.title: Locate the electron first, then examine the oscillator
sections.text: Conditional displacement divides the joint correlation by the electronic occupation of that site. The two plotted curves condition on the electron occupying site 0 or site 1, distinguishing local and remote vibrational clouds. Conditional quantities are undefined when the occupation probability is nearly zero; the interface leaves them blank.

sections.title: Connection to the density-matrix course
sections.text: Take partial trace for the oscillator to get the electron reduction density matrix . In the non-degenerate zero-temperature overall pure state, the electron reduced purity is lower than 1, indicating that the electron and oscillator are entanglement . Strictly the degenerate ground states of t=0 and Δ=0 are mixed by the program with equal weights. At this time, the low purity may also come from classical mixing and cannot be directly used as the amount of entanglement .

lessons.title: The result is calculated very accurately, why may it still not converge?
lessons.summary: Check energy changes, local observables, and highest-phonon-level probabilities together to identify finite-basis errors.

sections.title: The space of each oscillator is infinite
sections.text: A harmonic oscillator’s phonon number is unbounded. The browser experiment truncates each oscillator to occupations from 0 to a maximum and fully diagonalizes that finite matrix. The maximum input cutoff is 10; an extra comparison uses 11, giving maximum dimension 288.

sections.title: variational energy approaches from above
sections.text: Increasing the truncation enlarges the nested variational space, so the ground state energy cannot be increased (floating point errors are allowed). The program automatically compares the energies of two adjacent cutoffs, simultaneously comparing electron occupancy, phonon occupancy, and electron-displacement correlation.

sections.title: The highest level probability exposes the truncated tail
sections.text: If the highest allowed phonon layer still has a significant probability, truncated edges are affecting the wave function. The current diagnosis requires that the energy change is less than 10⁻⁴eV, the change of the specified local quantity is less than 0.01, and the top-level probability of each oscillator is less than 10⁻³. Passing the neighbor check is still not a strict global error bound.
sections.formula: P_i(N_{max})=Σ_(other degrees of freedom)|ψ|² (oscillator i fixed at its highest retained level)

sections.title: Scan cannot follow the conclusion of a point
sections.text: The sweep fixes the current truncation, and the phonon number generally increases as the coupling increases so that each point shows the highest level probability. Only the current parameters are additionally calculated for higher cutoffs. A small matrix residual only means that the matrix has been solved correctly, but it does not guarantee that the truncated phonon space is irrelevant.

lessons.title: Superposition, mixtures and partial traces
lessons.summary: uses the same local measurement results to identify different global quantum states.

sections.title: What information does density matrix retain?
sections.text: Pure states are written as outer products, and statistical mixtures are written as weighted sums of outer products. The diagonal elements are the measured probabilities in a given basis, and the off-diagonal elements contain coherence; change of basis will change the matrix appearance but not the purity.

sections.title: Superposition is not a classical random choice
sections.text: A +x pure state and an equal mixture of ↑ and ↓ each give half probabilities in z measurements; the former gives a definite positive x result, while the latter remains random. Compare complete density matrices rather than just one set of populations.

sections.title: When only observing A, find partial trace for B
sections.text: The double spin singlet state is an overall pure state, but the reduced state of either side is I/2. The omission of the other side does not mean that the whole was subjected to classical random mixing.

sections.title: The same local state does not guarantee the same overall state entanglement
sections.text: Both singlet and antiparallel classical equal-weighted mixtures have S(ρ_A)=1 bit; their overall purity is 1 and 1/2 respectively, and their negativity is 1/2 and 0 respectively. Local entropy directly quantifies this partitioning entanglement only when the ensemble is pure.

lessons.title: From Rabi Oscillations to Relaxation with decoherence
lessons.summary: First establish a dissipation-free benchmark, and then observe the population loss and coherence loss separately.

sections.title: First fix the unit of rotation angle
sections.text: Here Ω and Δ are coefficients of H/ℏ in rad/ns, and time uses ns. Starting from ↑ at resonance, the ↑ probability follows cos²(Ωt/2), reaching zero during each oscillation. Angular frequency and ordinary frequency differ by a factor of 2π.

sections.title: Amplitude damping from ↑ to ↓
sections.text: Choose C₁=√γ₁ |↓⟩⟨↑|. Without driving, ↑ population decays at rate γ₁. The channel direction is fixed and does not automatically reverse with the sign of detuning.

sections.title: Pure dephasing removes coherence in a fixed basis
sections.text: selects C_φ=√(γ_φ/2) σ_z; when there is no transverse drive, the diagonal element remains unchanged, and the non-diagonal element envelope is attenuated according to γ_φ. The single spin Bloch vector shrinks from the sphere to the z-axis.

sections.title: T₁ and T₂ are not two arbitrary independent fitting parameters
sections.text: This channel convention provides the longitudinal and transverse envelopes of single spin without drive and without exchange. In the presence of driving and double-spin coupling, the complete curve is not necessarily single exponential.

lessons.title: From the CG coupled basis to exchange-generated entanglement
lessons.summary: Decompose ↑↓ into singlet and triplet states and observe how the relative phase forms entanglement .

sections.title: Select coupling basis to explain evolution
sections.text: consists of two spin 1/2s S=0 and S=1. The antiparallel direct product state contains both singlet and triplet states; each component obtains different phases under isotropic exchange.

sections.title: The exchange energy level difference determines the beat frequency
sections.text: This module J is already the angular frequency, the singlet state H/ℏ eigenvalue is −3J/4, and the triplet state is J/4. After removing the global phase, evolution starts from ↑↓ between two antiparallel configurations.

sections.title: Local entropy of a pure state can reveal entanglement
sections.text: When Jt=π/2, the two configurations are equally weighted but have relative phases, the overall configuration is still pure, and the local configuration is I/2. When Jt=π, the system becomes another antiparallel direct product state, and entanglement is zero again.

sections.title: Mixed state requires another look at entanglement criterion
sections.text: Doing a partial transpose of B on a double spin, the sum of the absolute values ​​of negative eigenvalues ​​gives negativity. It applies to the 2×2 mixed state here; don't think of the local entropy alone as the mixed state entanglement .

lessons.title: From model convention to credible evolution results
lessons.summary: distinguishes between initial state temperature, phenomenological environment and numerical sampling, and checks the physical properties of the results.

sections.title: The initial thermal state is different from the ambient temperature
sections.text: thermalScale sets only the initial Gibbs weights for the current H. At zero, the program equally averages the complete ground-state subspace within a tolerance of 10⁻¹⁰ rad/ns. It does not automatically determine relaxation rates or impose detailed balance.

sections.title: Local channels do not automatically thermalize a coupled system
sections.text: The ↑→↓ and σ_z channels are defined in a fixed local basis. With driving or exchange, they need not induce transitions between energy eigenstates of the full H. The chosen γ₁ and γ_φ are not a complete microscopic description of a real material’s bath.

sections.title: Check both trace and positive semidefiniteness
sections.text: density matrix must be Hermitian , the trace is 1 and the eigenvalue is non-negative. The program reports full trajectory errors without patching dynamics by renormalizing or removing negative eigenvalues. Very small negative values ​​may be floating point errors, but obviously negative values ​​should be rejected.

sections.title: Sparse sampling and solver errors are different issues
sections.text: A constant generator propagates by a matrix exponential and can be solved at specified times. Sparse times can miss plotted oscillations; more samples should restore detail without changing the physical state at the same time.

lessons.title: From matrix identities to coefficient constraints
lessons.summary: The two components here form a real-spin doublet with common inversion parity. Pauli matrices transform as an axial vector. Replacing them by arbitrary orbitals requires specifying new representation matrices.

sections.title: First fix the representation space
sections.text: The two components here form a real-spin doublet with common inversion parity. Pauli matrices transform as an axial vector. Replacing them by arbitrary orbitals requires specifying new representation matrices.

sections.title: Compares the coefficients of all momentums
sections.text: The second-order two-dimensional polynomial has 6 monomials, each multiplied by 4 Hermitian basis matrices, for a total of 24 real coefficients. generator gives homogeneous linear constraints; energy cannot be compared just at a few high symmetry points.

sections.title: Find the allowed space first, then project
sections.text: Orthogonally projects the input coefficients into the null space of the constraint matrix. Combinations between coefficients may be required: a single k_x σ_y does not independently satisfy the C₄ rotation, while a Rashba combination does.

sections.title: View the meaning of projection
sections.text: workshop provides each front and rear coefficient, independent dimension, complete polynomial residual and curve near Γ. The null-space solution is numerical; the coefficient projection relies on the declared monomial Euclidean metric and cannot be treated as a material parameter fit.

lessons.title: Why does the inversion add time reversal to eliminate the spin splitting here?
lessons.summary: For the true spin half, time reversal contains complex conjugation , squared to −1. The scalar part is even for momentum and the spin part is odd.

sections.title: time reversal reverse spin
sections.text: For the true spin half, time reversal contains complex conjugation , squared to −1. The scalar part is even for momentum and the spin part is odd.

sections.title: Inversion does not invert axial vector spin
sections.text: The two states in this workshop have the same parity, and the inversion is expressed as a common positive or negative unit matrix. The inversion constraint makes the spin part also an even function.

sections.title: The same item is odd and even at the same time
sections.text: The spin part disappears after the two conditions are combined, so the two energy bands are degenerate at each k. This conclusion depends on the homoparity two-state space used and cannot be copied to any multi-orbital effective model.

sections.title: switch and group name must be consistent
sections.text: After turning off mirroring or rotating, the page only claims to retain the remaining generator . Adding additional inversion may expand the symmetry group, and we cannot simply call it the original C₄ᵥ.

lessons.title: Identify magnetic gap opening through controlled comparisons
lessons.summary: Rotation about z allows for the constant σ_z; the xz mirror inverts the z component of axial vector and time reversal also inverts it. Only when the corresponding restrictions are lifted and m is entered can it be retained.

sections.title: retains the constant term during rotation
sections.text: Rotation about z allows for the constant σ_z; the xz mirror inverts the z component of axial vector and time reversal also inverts it. Only when the corresponding restrictions are lifted and m is entered can it be retained.

sections.title: only changes one switch
sections.text: Fix the "keep rotation only" result to A, and then enable only time reversal to calculate B. Compare Γ point splitting with the same k path; do not change m and generator at the same time.

sections.title: Dispersion is not equal to complete topology diagnosis
sections.text: This low-order Γ neighborhood model does not have full Brillouin zone and lattice regularization. Even if the mass term appears, the Chern number of the material cannot be determined from this local energy band curve.

sections.title: Return to matrix conditions to explain the phenomenon
sections.text: The project conclusion should write down the destroyed generator , the changed coefficients and the physical consequences. If the graph appears to be degenerate, it is still necessary to check the complete coefficient constraints to avoid accidental degeneracy of values ​​or paths.

exercises.title: Read local spectra from a noninteracting dimer
exercises.prompt: takes t=1 eV, U=Δ=μ=0, and N↑=N↓=1; first use local probes, and then change to Fourier probes.

steps.prompt: Which sector should you enter after removing an up-spin electron?
steps.hint: Only the electron count of the annihilated spin species changes.
steps.explanation: c↑Reduce the number of upper spin electrons from 1 to 0; the corresponding final states come from different particle number sectors, and you cannot only read the excitation energy of the initial state sector.

steps.prompt: Where do the local probes have peaks and what is their weight?
steps.hint: The bonding and antibonding energies of single particles are −t and +t, and the local orbitals occupy half of each.
steps.explanation: fills the bonding orbitals; the removed peak is at −1 eV, the added peak is at +1 eV, and the total weight is 1.

steps.prompt: only changed μ to 0.3 eV. Which change is correct?
steps.hint: μ is subtracted from each single particle peak coordinate.
choices: The number of electrons increases automatically
Both peaks shift to the right by 0.3 eV
The two peaks change to −1.3 and 0.7 eV, and the weight remains unchanged.
steps.explanation: Here μ only sets the zero point of the spectrum; the initial states of fixed N↑ and N↓ remain unchanged, and it is not an automatic doping calculation.

steps.prompt: Restore μ=0 and change it to q=0 normalized Fourier probe. What will you see?
steps.hint: The same phase addition of two stations selects the bonding orbit.
choices: Only a removal peak at E=−1 eV, with weight 1
Add only peak E=+1 eV with weight 1
steps.explanation: q=0 probe is completely in the occupied bonding mode; the Pauli principle prevents the addition of same-spin electrons.

exercises.title: Why does the same dimer have different dynamic energy gaps?
exercises.prompt: Take the half-filled dimer of t=1 eV, U=4 eV, and Δ=0, and use the q a/π=1 probe.

steps.prompt: density or S_z response change the total number of electrons?
steps.hint: Both operators contain a creation and an annihilation operation.
choices: No, the final state is still in the same particle number sector
steps.explanation: Response and single-particle addition/removal spectra use different operators and final spaces, so energy positions alone do not make them interchangeable.

steps.prompt: For D=√32 eV, what is the energy of the spin peak?
steps.hint: Calculate (D−U)/2.
steps.explanation: spin peak connects the lowest singlet state to the triplet state; here it is approximately 0.828427 eV.

steps.prompt: Under the same parameters, what is the energy of the charge peak?
steps.hint: Calculate (D+U)/2 this time.
steps.explanation: The charge operator couples to an odd-parity doubly occupied state, with excitation energy about 4.828427 eV, distinct from the spin peak.

steps.prompt: If q is changed to 0, what should be the total connected density spectrum of fixed N?
steps.hint: The total density in this sector is the N times identity operator.
choices: retains the connected zero-energy peak of weight N²
steps.explanation: δN=N−⟨N⟩I=0; After the coherent average background is subtracted, there is no total density fluctuation for a fixed number of particles.

exercises.title: Don’t mistake linewidth, degeneracy and peak height for physical conclusions
exercises.prompt: First look at the spin response in the strict atomic limit, and then compare the two displayed half-widths of the same single particle spectrum.

steps.prompt: At t=0,U>0,N↑=N↓=1, how should the two separated-electron ground states be handled?
steps.hint: results should not rely on degenerate bases selected by diagonalization.
choices: Choose any one and call it the only ground state
Equally weighted average in the degenerate subspace of this sector
steps.explanation: The ground-state mixture at strictly t=0 differs from the singlet selected as t→0⁺; calculations retain the declared fixed sector and degenerate averaging.

steps.prompt: The q a/π=1 longitudinal probe has mean zero. What is the connected spectrum’s zero-energy weight?
steps.hint: The probe value for two separated configurations is ±1/√2.
steps.explanation: is 0 and the square mean is 1/2; the degenerate mixed state still has zero energy fluctuations and cannot be deleted uniformly.

steps.prompt: Only doubles the Lorentz half-width eta, which quantity should remain unchanged?
steps.hint: eta acts on the display core of each discrete peak.
choices: All pixel values within the limited drawing window
steps.explanation: The discrete matrix element weight has nothing to do with eta; the peak height and the limited window area may change, so the occupancy number cannot be determined by the peak height.

steps.prompt: The area of ​​the single particle drawing window is slightly less than 1, but the discrete weight sum is 1. What should be checked first?
steps.hint: Lorentz line has a tail outside any finite window.
choices: Check window tails and sampling accuracy against the reported analytical area
Announcement of Violation of Fermi Anti- commutation relations
steps.explanation: Report full sum rules separately from finite-window integrals. Enlarging the window or refining the mesh diagnoses display error; renormalization must not hide the difference.

exercises.title: Checkpointing from uncoupled limits
exercises.prompt: Taking t=1, ℏω=1 and g=Δ=0 eV, the maximum number of phonon per vibrator is 6.

steps.explanation: 2×7×7=98; the two oscillators cannot share a single number-state label.

steps.hint: The electron bonding state energy is −t, and the oscillators are all in vacuum.
steps.explanation: electron energy −1 eV, b†b of both oscillators is 0.

steps.prompt: What is the electron reduced purity at this time?
steps.hint: The overall state is the direct product of the electron and oscillator states.
steps.explanation: Tracing the oscillator does not cause the electrons to become a mixed state, so Tr(ρ_e²)=1.

steps.prompt: What does this module’s added g term directly modulate?
steps.hint: The coupling term is gΣ_i n_i X_i.
steps.explanation: This is Holstein onsite coupling. Bond-displacement modulation of hopping is a different coupling type, so their parameters cannot be interchanged.

exercises.title: Complete the square and then identify the conditional vibration cloud
exercises.prompt: First take t=0, ℏω=1 and g=0.5 eV, with the electron known to occupy one site.

steps.prompt: What is the reduction in ground state energy caused by the occupied oscillator?
steps.hint: Completing the square gives the constant term −g²/(ℏω).
steps.explanation: −0.5²/1=−0.25 eV, electronic site potential not included.

steps.prompt: What is the ⟨X⟩ of the occupied oscillator?
steps.hint: The shifted annihilation operator defines the oscillator vacuum, with ⟨b⟩=−g/(ℏω).
steps.explanation: X=b+b†, so ⟨X⟩=−2g/(ℏω)=−1, dimensionless.

steps.prompt: After restoring hopping and site-exchange symmetry, what does uniform electron density establish?
steps.hint: The density is a single expected value, and the conditional association also contains joint information.
choices: There must be no electron–phonon correlations
Need to continue to check ⟨n_i X_j⟩ and conditional displacement
steps.explanation: Uniform density can coexist with co-delocalized vibration clouds and cannot be judged by density alone.

steps.prompt: If the program averages the degenerate ground states equally, can low electron purity be directly quantified entanglement ?
steps.hint: as a whole density matrix may be in mixed state.
choices: No, classic mixing will also reduce the purity.
Yes, as long as the phonon number is non-zero
steps.explanation: Only under the overall pure state condition, the reduced mixing degree can directly characterize the two-part entanglement ; the mixed state requires additional criteria.

exercises.title: Make truncation error a checkable experimental variable
exercises.prompt: Run the deliberately insufficient-cutoff preset, then gradually increase each oscillator’s maximum phonon occupation.

steps.prompt: How should the variational ground energy change when the phonon cutoff is increased?
steps.hint: Adding basis vectors does not remove previously available trial states.
steps.explanation: The variational minimum of the nested space does not increase; the size of the change reflects truncation sensitivity.

steps.prompt: Which diagnostic most directly checks whether phonon probability reaches the truncation boundary?
steps.hint: Checks the last allowed number state.
choices: Probability of the highest phonon layer
steps.explanation: Higher phonon states that are not included may be important when the top level still has significant weight.

steps.prompt: An eigenproblem residual is 10⁻¹². Does this alone prove the phonon cutoff is sufficient?
steps.hint: Residuals test the finite matrix already constructed.
choices: only needs the matrix dimension to be greater than 20
No, we need to expand the truncation comparison.
steps.explanation: finite matrix can be solved extremely accurately while still missing important high phonon configurations.

steps.prompt: After the current g point passes the adjacent truncation diagnosis, will the entire g scan pass automatically?
steps.hint: scan points have different vibration clouds and phonon distributions.
choices: No, you must check point by point
Yes, the truncation is the same number
Yes, as long as the energy at both ends is smooth
steps.explanation: The control of the current point cannot replace other points; this experiment scan reports the highest level probability of each point. If necessary, select this parameter separately for double truncation.

exercises.title: Identify different global states behind the same local state
exercises.prompt: Compare the singlet and antiparallel classical-mixture presets.

steps.prompt: What is the singlet's global purity?
steps.hint: pure density matrix meets ρ²=ρ.
steps.explanation: singlet state is the normalized pure state, Trρ²=1.

steps.prompt: What is A’s reduced density matrix after tracing out B?
steps.hint: The two spin outcomes are equally probable, and tracing out the other spin leaves no local coherence.
steps.explanation: ρ_A=I/2, so the local entropy is 1 bit.

steps.prompt: Does antiparallel classical equal-weighted mixing also have local entropy 1 bit?
steps.hint: Take partial trace for two antiparallel direct product states and then average them.
choices: has, but it is separable classic mix
steps.explanation: It is the same as the singlet local state, but with an overall negativity of 0.

steps.prompt: Which quantity distinguishes these two examples of entanglement ?
steps.hint: uses dual-spin partially transposed spectra.
choices: Local entropy only: both are 1 entanglement
steps.explanation: Negativity distinguishes the two; local entropy is not a separate entanglement quantity for general mixed states.

exercises.title: Distinguish T₁, T₂, and pure dephasing
exercises.prompt: takes the single spin without driver γ₁=0.4 and γ_φ=0.1 ns⁻¹.

steps.prompt: What is T₁?
steps.hint: T₁=1/γ₁。

steps.prompt: What is the transverse-envelope decay rate?
steps.hint: γ₂=γ₁/2+γ_φ。

steps.prompt: With only pure dephasing and Ω=0, what happens to z populations?
steps.hint: The σ_z channel commutes with the projectors of this basis.
steps.explanation: Pure dephasing damps off-diagonal entries without directly changing populations under these conditions.

steps.prompt: For drive=1 rad/ns, what is the ordinary frequency?
steps.hint: angular frequency divided by 2π.
steps.explanation: H/ℏ uses angular frequency and cannot directly read 1 rad/ns as 1 GHz.

exercises.title: From the exchange energy level to the maximum entanglement moment
exercises.prompt: Take J=1 rad/ns, Ω=Δ=δ=γ₁=γ_φ=0, initial state ↑↓.

steps.prompt: What are the H/ℏ eigenvalues ​​of the singlet and triplet states?
steps.hint: Use S_A·S_B=[S²−S_A²−S_B²]/2.
steps.explanation: The two spins 1/2 have S_A²=S_B²=3/4 and S is 0 or 1.

steps.prompt: When did the first equal weighting of two antiparallel configurations occur?
steps.hint: cos²(t/2)=sin²(t/2)。
steps.explanation: When t=π/2 ns, both probabilities are 1/2.

steps.prompt: What are the overall purity, local entropy and negativity at this time?
steps.hint: Unitary evolution preserves purity, and the local state is I/2.
steps.explanation: Overall pure and maximal entanglement ; local mixture produced by entanglement .

steps.prompt: Will entanglement continue to grow when it reaches t=π ns?
steps.hint: At this time cos(t/2)=0.
choices: No, it becomes ↓↑ direct product state, and the negativity returns to 0
steps.explanation: There is a coherent round trip in finite double spins, and entanglement does not have to grow monotonically.

exercises.title: Examine thermal initial states, dissipation, and numerical conclusions
exercises.prompt: Enable local dissipation for a thermal initial state, then compare sparse and dense time sampling.

steps.prompt: thermalScale determines what?
steps.hint: It goes into the initial Gibbs weights.
steps.explanation: The initial state temperature scale and dissipation channel parameters are input independently.

steps.prompt: Does the local ↑→↓ channel guarantee that an exchange-coupled system approaches a Gibbs state at the same temperature?
steps.hint: Check whether detailed balance is constructed from the full energy-level differences.
choices: guarantees that any Lindblad equation is thermalized
Not guaranteed, this channel does not apply this detailed balance
is guaranteed as long as the trace is 1
steps.explanation: Complete positivity and trace preservation do not ensure thermal equilibrium for a specified Hamiltonian.

steps.prompt: has trace 1, but has obvious negative eigenvalues. Can it be regarded as a physical state?
steps.hint: The probability cannot be negative.
choices: Yes, just delete the negative values manually
No, it is necessary to find out the numerical or model errors.
steps.explanation: Hermiticity, normalization, and positive semidefiniteness are all required.

steps.prompt: What should be the main changes when increasing the time sampling point?
steps.hint: For a constant generator, propagation to the same time is given by the same matrix exponential.
choices: Display details; the states at the same time should be consistent within the tolerance
steps.explanation: Sparse sampling can miss oscillations, but changing sampling cannot change the underlying physical evolution.

Only look at the Γ point

exercises.title: Why the inversion adds time reversal to eliminate spin splitting here: step-by-step verification
exercises.prompt: First deduce based on the representation and generator , and then run the preset verification in the workshop.

exercises.prompt: First deduce based on the representation and generator , and then run the preset verification in the workshop.

cases.title: Molecular dimer: from bonding energy level to electron increase and decrease spectrum
cases.summary: Place the local and bonding/antibonding probes on the same dimer and compare the peak positions and visible weights for U=0 and U>0.
cases.assumption: Two abstract orbitals borrowed from the molecular dimer image; no organic salts were fitted, no real photoelectron dipole matrix elements, surface effects or experimental absolute cross sections were calculated.

cases.title: Spin and charge probes of the same local correlation system
cases.summary: For the same half-filled dimer, compare the low-energy spin peak and the high-energy charge peak, and use isochronous correlation to verify the spectrum area.
cases.assumption: This dimer only shows that different operators detect different excitations; the curve cannot be directly marked as a real neutron, RIXS or optical experimental section, nor can the long-range magnetic order be predicted from the two sites.

cases.title: Finite correlation loop: how spectral weights rearrange with probe momentum
cases.summary: Variation of the normalized Fourier probe on a four-site periodic ring to observe the connection between allowed transitions, peak area, and local occupancy.
cases.assumption: Four stations have only a limited set of strictly allowed momentums; the other q are probes with specified phases. Discrete peaks, broadening and finite energy gaps cannot be regarded as infinite system Mott phase diagrams or real ARPES energy bands.

cases.title: Carriers and local vibrations in molecular dimers
cases.summary: uses local orbits and oscillators to illustrate that electrons can also carry vibration clouds when delocalized, comparing no coupling and limited coupling.
cases.assumption: Two abstract sites and given energy parameters, does not fit the vibration frequency, transition or spectrum of a specific molecule; fixed single electron.

cases.title: Comparison of the mechanisms of local coupling and conjugated chain bond coupling
cases.summary: Starting from Holstein's site energy modulation, compare the alternating bonds of the SSH chain with domain wall ; first identify which matrix element the coupling occurs.
cases.assumption: This comparison concerns the mechanism only. The two-site Holstein result is not identified with a self-consistent polyacetylene structure, an SSH domain wall, or a physical polaron radius.
links: SSH domain wall and local state

cases.title: Numerical convergence experiment on strongly vibrating clouds
cases.summary: Compares exact eigenresiduals, top-level probabilities, and adjacent truncation energy changes at larger g/(ℏω).
cases.assumption: intentionally contains under-truncated parameters to identify numerical artefacts; unconverged curves cannot be interpreted as real material phase transitions or quantitative spectra.

cases.title: Coherence and dissipation of effective spin resonance
cases.summary: Connect the magnetic resonance class with Rabi evolution using an effective spin, switching relaxation and pure decoherence respectively.
cases.assumption: parameters are teaching values; T₁ and T₂ are not automatically inferred from material structure or frequency domain line width, and do not include powder averaging, pulse echo or noise spectrum fitting.

cases.title: Dual spin exchange and controllable entanglement
cases.summary: Use two effective spins to explain exchange levels, relative phases, and entanglement generation, then return to the Hubbard dimer to discuss the low-energy approximation.
cases.assumption: The two-spin model retains only one spin 1/2 per site, whereas the Hubbard model includes charge fluctuations. Their exchange scales can be compared only in the appropriate low-energy, large-U regime.

cases.title: The same local measurement is associated with different global
cases.summary: Compare singlet state and classical mixing; the local Bloch sphere center is the same, but the overall density matrix and entanglement criteria are different.
cases.assumption: This is a comparison of two ideal states with distinguishable spins; the local entropy of the mixed state is not directly interpreted as entanglement , nor does it predict the macroscopic quantum resources of real materials.
links: Pure state and mixed state class

cases.title: interface inversion violation and Rashba type term
cases.summary: Understanding allowed linear spin-momentum coupling at surfaces or interfaces with the C₄ᵥ two-state model.
cases.assumption: Reduced k, schematic coefficients and true spin double states with same parity; not the fitted energy band of a specific interface.

cases.title: How magnetic items are limited by mirrors and time reversal
cases.summary: After closing generator , trace the σ_z coefficients and Γ point splitting to distinguish the spectral consequences and constraint sources.
cases.assumption: The complete small representation of magnetic space group is not constructed; generator is only imposed on the declared 2×2 model.
